Perikatan Nasional Sedia Masuk Gelanggang PRN Johor

Perikatan Nasional (PN) mengambil maklum pengumuman pembubaran Dewan Undangan Negeri Johor bagi memberi laluan kepada Pilihan Raya Negeri. 

Pilihan raya bukan sekadar pertandingan politik, tetapi medan untuk menawarkan penyelesaian yang lebih baik kepada rakyat khususnya dalam isu kos sara hidup, peluang pekerjaan, pembangunan ekonomi negeri, integriti pentadbiran dan masa depan negara.

Sehubungan itu, saya menyeru seluruh kepimpinan, jentera dan ahli-ahli parti komponen Perikatan Nasional agar memberikan fokus sepenuhnya terhadap persiapan menghadapi pilihan raya ini dengan semangat kebersamaan, disiplin serta kesatuan tindakan.

Perikatan Nasional akan memasuki gelanggang pilihan raya ini dengan penuh tanggungjawab, matang dan profesional serta meletakkan kepentingan rakyat sebagai keutamaan. 

Saya juga berharap seluruh jentera dapat mengelakkan sebarang bentuk provokasi melampau, politik kebencian dan perpecahan, sebaliknya menampilkan politik yang lebih tenang, berfakta dan berorientasikan solusi.

Insya-Allah, dengan kerjasama semua pihak serta sokongan rakyat, Perikatan Nasional akan terus membawa agenda pentadbiran yang stabil, bersih dan prihatin demi masa depan Johor dan Malaysia yang lebih baik.

If election fever is a thing, the temperature in Malaysia saw a sharp spike over the weekend.

It began on Saturday when Barisan Nasional announced it would contest all 56 seats in the next Johor state election, essentially distancing itself from Pakatan Harapan - its unity government partner at the federal level and in several states including Johor.

PH folks, already gathering in the southern state for their major national convention, rallied hard on Sunday. Top brass framed it as a challenge thrown down. PM Anwar Ibrahim warned that elections are his call and he is prepared to send the entire country to the polls. Before the night ended, the chief minister of Melaka, another BN-UMNO stronghold, hinted that Melaka could also see an election in the next few months.

Further up in Selangor, taking the stage quite literally at a local performing arts centre, two PKR MPs who were ex-ministers in PM Anwar’s cabinet announced that they will vacate their parliamentary seats as they “adopted” a different political party - one that was unheard of prior to this announcement. Kamikaze mission, they called it.

CNA’s Malaysia team was activated in both states and got a taste (or reminder) of what the next few months could look like. Good thing we all love election coverage. 

Our senior correspondents Melissa and Afifah brought us the latest and, as always, allowed me to live vicariously through them. Texting both correspondents while fleshing out lines, vetting copies, sorting out tech issues and watching simultaneous livestreams truly tested my multitasking abilities.

Credit also goes to Ahmad Asraf Suhaimi, Mohd Afzal Idrose, Lancelot and PUUNITHA - the BTS powerhouses (behind-the-scenes, not the K-pop band).

I have full faith that our team is also prepared for when the entire country goes to the polls. No kamikaze. Just gambatte.

I spoke with Aqil Haziq Mahmud on the PAS-Bersatu rift, which may give Anwar some political breathing room but is not enough on its own to justify snap polls, especially amid cost-of-living pressures and tensions within his own camp.
For PN, the bigger risk is credibility: a coalition visibly divided risks looking less like a government-in-waiting and more like a temporary electoral vehicle.

“The PAS-Bersatu fracture is politically useful to Anwar, but not enough on its own to justify snap polls,” said Asrul Sani, associate vice-president at strategic advisory firm The Asia Group.

“Anwar still faces complications within his own camp, including UMNO-PKR seat tensions, Rafizi’s Bersama project, and possible PKR defections.”

The analyst was referring to how the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) - the lynchpin party of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition - has declared it will contest all seats in the upcoming Johor state election despite being in the unity government with PH.
-
Beyond political dynamics, Asrul from The Asia Group said the bigger issue for Anwar is the economy.

“Rising prices, cost-of-living pressures, and subsidy rationalisation make an early election risky. The government may be able to stretch existing subsidies into next year, but only with continued fiscal pressure and gradual adjustments,” he said.

“Snap polls could backfire if voters see them as a mandate for unpopular cuts. Voters ultimately judge governments on what they feel in their wallets.”
-
“PAS has a more defensible core. Its base in Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis is ideologically loyal and less dependent on coalition arrangements.”

If Bersatu goes solo, it would need to broaden its reach, possibly by engaging Sabah and Sarawak-based opposition parties or positioning itself as the anchor of a wider non-PH alternative, Asrul said.

“PAS, meanwhile, would likely double down on Islamic identity rhetoric together with cost-of-living frustrations. Its strength rests in ideological loyalty, religious credibility and grassroots mobilisation,” he said.

While Asrul feels a complete break is not inevitable, he said the political value of a PAS-Bersatu partnership is “clearly diminishing”.

“For PN, the real danger is credibility. A coalition visibly at odds with itself stops looking like a government in waiting and starts looking like a temporary electoral vehicle,” he added.

“PN may survive in form, but its internal trust and strategic coherence would be badly weakened.”

Fresh news flow on the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) has boosted interest in the property sector – particularly in Johor-centric property names – as the Johor state elections draw nearer, says CIMB Research.

In a research note, CIMB Research further noted that the JS-SEZ investment blueprint and master plan are being reviewed by the National Investment Council before being tabled to the Cabinet for final approval.

Initially slated for launch on March 30, 2026, the JS-SEZ is now set to be rolled out by the first half of financial year 2026 following further refinements to its content.

“While the JS-SEZ is still a work in progress, we opine that the crystallisation of a formalised agreement marks another significant step that strengthens cross-border economic integration between Malaysia and Singapore. 

“Broadly, the JS-SEZ is projected to generate RM260bil in gross domestic product for Johor by 2030, and we expect this wealth creation to trickle down into the state’s property sector,” said CIMB Research.

Beyond the JS-SEZ, the research house said the property sector’s sentiment-driven re-rating has been boosted by investor repositioning into stocks seen as potential beneficiaries of the MY Value Up programme launched on April 20, 2026, although details of its mechanism remain unclear.

“Among property stocks or companies with real estate exposure within our coverage, Gamuda, IJM Corp, Sime Darby Property, SP Setia, Eco World and Sunway meet the minimum RM4bil market cap requirement, securing their place in the list of 88 companies that have been selected for this voluntary programme,” it added.

However, CIMB Research noted that further delays to the signing of the JS-SEZ’s formal agreement could dampen investor appetite.
Additionally, a protracted war in West Asia could lead to higher construction costs, supply chain disruptions, and curtail inbound investments into the JS-SEZ region, it added.

“Domestically, investment decisions or approvals may only be finalised upon the conclusion of the upcoming Johor state elections.

“It is worth noting that the incumbent state government’s term is scheduled to end in April 2027,” said CIMB Research. — Bernama

PRN JOHOR 2026: BN JOHOR ‘GO SOLO’

Halim Tuah
Pemerhati Politik & Hal Ehwal Strategik
1 Jun 2026

Pembubaran DUN Johor hari ini bukan sekadar membuka laluan kepada satu lagi Pilihan Raya Negeri. Pada hemat saya sebagai pemerhati politik, ia merupakan satu langkah politik yang telah dikira dengan teliti oleh kepimpinan Johor untuk mendapatkan mandat baharu ketika mereka merasakan kedudukan mereka berada pada tahap yang paling kukuh.

Apa yang lebih menarik ialah persoalan sama ada Barisan Nasional akan terus bergandingan dengan Pakatan Harapan atau memilih untuk bergerak secara solo. Jika BN Johor benar-benar mengambil keputusan untuk bertanding bersendirian, ia memberi isyarat bahawa mereka yakin jenama BN di Johor masih mempunyai kekuatan tersendiri dan tidak lagi mahu bergantung kepada mana-mana rakan politik untuk mendapatkan mandat rakyat.

Hakikatnya, sentimen semasa menunjukkan kerajaan Persekutuan sedang berhadapan pelbagai cabaran. Isu kos sara hidup, tekanan ekonomi, persepsi rakyat terhadap prestasi pentadbiran serta pelbagai polemik politik yang berlarutan sedikit sebanyak memberi kesan kepada sokongan terhadap Pakatan Harapan. Dalam keadaan sebegini, tidak mustahil terdapat pihak dalam UMNO dan BN yang berpendapat bahawa membawa imej Kerajaan Perpaduan ke medan pilihan raya negeri mungkin lebih menjadi liabiliti berbanding aset.

Johor selama ini dikenali sebagai kubu tradisi UMNO dan BN. Jika BN berjaya memperoleh kemenangan besar secara solo, mesej politik yang akan dihantar bukan sahaja kepada rakyat Johor, malah kepada seluruh negara. Ia akan menjadi bukti bahawa UMNO masih mempunyai kekuatan akar umbi yang signifikan tanpa perlu bergantung kepada PH. Kemenangan sedemikian juga berpotensi mengubah landskap perbincangan politik nasional menjelang PRU16.

Malaysian politics is starting to look less like strategy…
 and more like a never-ending group project with too many “future prime ministers” in one WhatsApp group 😅

PAS reviewing Bersatu.
 Anwar vs Rafizi heating up.
 Johor becoming a testing ground for a new party.

At this point, Malaysian political chess is getting more dramatic than some Netflix series 🍿

But beyond the headlines, there’s something more worrying happening:

The Malay community keeps getting divided over politics.

Families stop talking.
 Friends become enemies.
 WhatsApp groups turn into war zones over party logos and politicians who may eventually sit together again after the election 🤝😂

That’s the irony of Malaysian politics.

In Malaysia, parties do not always win because they are stronger. Sometimes they win because their opponents are more divided.

And honestly… that statement feels very relevant today.

Johor is a perfect example.
 If multiple parties split the same voter base, the outcome may already be decided before the campaign even begins.

From a GE16 and Johor state election perspective, this is no longer just about ideology.
 It’s about mathematics, machinery, funding, and ego management.

Politics is important. Democracy matters. Healthy debates matter.

But when political loyalty becomes bigger than unity, society slowly pays the price.

As Muslims, we are taught that differences in opinion are normal.
 What should never become normal is turning politics into hatred.

Because at the end of the day:

Politicians may change alliances.
 Parties may split and reunite.
 But rakyat still wake up facing the same cost of living, same commitments, and same struggles.

Sometimes I feel Malaysians are not tired of politics.
 They are tired of endless political drama without enough solutions.

Politics should unite people around solutions — not divide communities over personalities.

Different opinions are healthy.
 Broken relationships are not.

In the end, after all the speeches, campaigns, flags, TikToks, and political chess moves…

We are still one Malaysia 🇲🇾
